extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists, literary authors, and readers interested in the craft and publication of fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative criteria for writing and publishing novels (especially realist, character-driven fiction and serialized work), including character consistency, depiction of moral issues, use of local colour, handling of periodicals, and how criticism and signature affect reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal of marriage and personal agency
rubrics_metrics.description: It must ever be wrong to force a girl into a marriage with a man she does not love,--and certainly the more so when there is another whom she does love.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use marriage as mere plot coercion; portray characters' marital choices sensitively and respect their emotional agency. If you intervene in plot to ‘save’ a character from a bad match, acknowledge moral complexity rather than forcing an unnatural resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depicting immoral behavior without endorsing it
rubrics_metrics.description: I made known nothing which the purest girl could not but have learned... and I certainly lent no attraction to the sin which I indicated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors may depict temptation or contemplated adultery so long as they do not glamorize the sin. Showing a wife's contemplation of adultery can be legitimate provided the depiction does not lend attraction to it and the moral consequences are clear — parallel to how clergy preach against adultery from the pulpit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character consistency with natural change
rubrics_metrics.description: I realised the necessity, not only of consistency,--which, had it been maintained by a hard exactitude, would have been untrue to nature,--but also of those changes which time always produces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain core characteristics across time (the selfish remain selfish, the false remain false) while allowing believable changes in expression, intensity, and the way traits are shown or hidden. Avoid rigid exactitude that would be 'untrue to nature.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowing character development across multiple works
rubrics_metrics.description: These people, as they grew in years, should encounter the changes which come upon us all; and I think that I have succeeded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When carrying characters across novels or a series, plan for how age, rank, experience and public role will alter their behaviour while keeping identity recognisable (e.g., Lady Glencora and the Duke of Omnium undergoing natural changes but remaining essentially the same persons).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and accessibility of sprawling series
rubrics_metrics.description: To carry out my scheme I have had to spread my picture over so wide a canvas that I cannot expect that any lover of such art should trouble himself to look at it as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about extending a story world across many long works if readers are unlikely to read them consecutively. Consider whether your narrative scope demands readership of multiple volumes and whether you can make each work stand alone or signal where continuity matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of fiction for social or political comment
rubrics_metrics.description: I was enabled from time to time to have in this way that fling at the political doings of the day which every man likes to take...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate political or social satire judiciously — occasional 'flings' can be satisfying, but be aware of venue and balance so the commentary does not overwhelm the fiction. Satire should arise from the work's perspective rather than dominate it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary qualities that mark a great novel
rubrics_metrics.description: I myself regard _Esmond_ as the greatest novel in the English language, basing that judgment upon the excellence of its language, on the clear individuality of the characters, on the truth of its delineations in regard to the time selected, and on its great pathos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate (and strive for) excellence of language, distinct individuality of characters, truthful and accurate depiction of the chosen time/setting, and genuine pathos. Exceptional scenes ('so told that even Scott has never equalled the telling') can lift a novel's stature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapting content to the publication's principles and audience
rubrics_metrics.description: He said that the story... he could not give to his readers in the pages of _Good Words_.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing for a particular periodical or publisher, respect their editorial principles and audience expectations. Material (e.g., dancing scenes, secular tone) that conflicts with a publication's stance may be refused; accept that one man's food is another's poison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thematic honesty / sustaining a premise
rubrics_metrics.description: Miss Mackenzie was written with a desire to prove that a novel may be produced without any love; but even in this attempt it breaks down before the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you set a thematic experiment (e.g., a novel without love), ensure the premise can be sustained through the narrative arc. Avoid premises that collapse under character needs or reader expectations; be honest about limits of conceit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial coherence for periodicals
rubrics_metrics.description: That theory of eclecticism was altogether impracticable... Such gentlemen have gone into the House of Commons, but they have not served their country much.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An editorial or organizational stance that tries to combine irreconcilable positions (neither conservative nor liberal, neither religious nor free-thinking) is impracticable. Define a clear editorial identity; eclecticism without a core principle tends to fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signing articles to increase accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: I wrote a paper advocating the signature of the authors to periodical writing... I think that the name of the author does tend to honesty, and that the knowledge that it will be inserted adds much to the author's industry and care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attaching authors' names to articles promotes responsibility, reduces illegitimate license and dishonest assertions, and tends to improve critical standards. Consider signatures especially where accountability and reader trust matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for literary criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Much of the literary criticism which we now have is very bad indeed;--so bad as to be open to the charge both of dishonesty and incapacity. Books are criticised without being read,--are criticised by favour,--and are trusted by editors to the criticism of the incompetent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should actually read the works they judge, be competent in the subject, and avoid bias or favouritism. Honest, qualified criticism is preferable even if it reduces the quantity of reviews; demand competence and accountability from reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pick appropriate venue for polemical arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: I felt that _The Fortnightly_ was hardly the place for the defence of the sport.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the readership and editorial sympathies of the venue when publishing polemical pieces; an argument is less effective (and may be refused) if the platform is unsympathetic to its stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptiveness to newspaper/periodical working conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: I had not taken to it early enough in life to learn its ways and bear its trammels... I was fidgety when any word was altered in accordance with the judgment of the editor... I wanted to select my own subjects,--not to have them selected for me; to write when I pleased,--and not when it suited others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you work on a newspaper or as a regular contributor, be prepared for editorial control, assigned topics, rigid schedules, and collaborative constraints. Some writers are unsuited to staff roles and should prefer freelance or book-length work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartiality and ethical restraint when judging acquaintances
rubrics_metrics.description: It was not open to me to whitewash with honesty him whom I did not find to be white; but there was no duty incumbent on me to declare what was his colour in my eyes,--no duty even to ascertain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid letting personal requests or friendships coerce public judgment. Do not feel obliged to publish a full verdict on acquaintances' conduct; maintain impartiality and consider whether public commentary is necessary or ethical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of anonymity and the power of name recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: I began a short tale called _Nina Balatka_... published anonymously... Blackwood... expressed an opinion that it would not from its style be discovered to have been written by me;--but it was discovered... It had no real success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that authorial reputation and name recognition strongly influence reception and sales. Anonymity can reveal whether work stands alone, but it often reduces commercial success; plan anonymity experiments with this in mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use local colour and on-location observation
rubrics_metrics.description: They were both written very quickly, but with a considerable amount of labour; and both were written immediately after visits to the towns in which the scenes are laid,--Prague, mainly, and Nuremberg.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visit locations or conduct direct research to capture local colour, authentic descriptions, and setting-specific detail. On-location observations can enrich scenes, lend verisimilitude, and differentiate style and storytelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balancing humour and pathos
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief merit of _The Claverings_ is in the genuine fun of some of the scenes. Humour has not been my forte... Her sorrow is, I think, pathetic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for genuine moments of humour and pathos appropriate to characters and plot. Even if humour is not a writer's strongest suit, well-observed comic or tragic scenes contribute to the story's appeal and emotional truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honest, measured advice to aspiring writers
rubrics_metrics.description: The judgment, whether cruel or tender, should not be ill-judgment. He who consents to sit as judge should have capacity for judging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When advising aspirants, be careful, competent and measured. Recognize the high failure rate in literature and avoid gratuitous cruelty; give honest counsel grounded in experience and the ability to evaluate specific effort.
